hints: Think about what you see at room temperature as you go down Group 17, chlorine is a pale green gas, so what happens to boiling point and colour intensity for the heavier halogens?
walkthrough:
Picture the group trend**
You already know chlorine is a green gas. Down the group London forces get stronger, so boiling points rise. That means bromine is condensed to a liquid and iodine is condensed all the way to a solid at room temperature.

Add the colours**
Colour gets darker down the group. Bromine is a dark red-brown fuming liquid, iodine is a grey-black shiny solid that gives a purple vapour.
Final answer: bromine: (dark / red-)brown liquid AND iodine: grey / black solid

hints: Look at the bond energy numbers in Table 3.1, 242 to 193 to 151, and think about what happens to atomic radius down Group 17.
Link larger atoms to the distance between the bonding pair and the nuclei and to how well the outer orbitals can overlap.
walkthrough:
State the trend from the data**
$242 > 193 > 151$ $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ for $\text{Cl-Cl}$, $\text{Br-Br}$, $\text{I-I}$. Less energy is needed to break the bond down the group, so bond strength decreases.

Why larger atoms give longer, weaker bonds**
Down the group the outer shell is further out, $n=3$ to $4$ to $5$. The atoms are larger, so the two nuclei sit further apart. The bonding pair is further from each nucleus and the large diffuse orbitals overlap less effectively. Electrostatic attraction between nuclei and shared pair falls, so the covalent bond is longer and weaker.

Final answer: Bond strength decreases down the group.
Atoms become larger down the group so the distance between the bonding electron pair and the nuclei increases / bond length increases / there is less effective orbital overlap, giving weaker attraction and a weaker bond.

hints: Recall that chlorine in water undergoes a disproportionation reaction with water itself, forming two acids, one containing only H and Cl.
Think about which chlorine-containing product is the disinfectant and what it does to microorganisms.
walkthrough:
Write the reaction with water**
Chlorine does not just dissolve, it reacts:
$$\text{Cl}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{HCl} + \text{HOCl}$$
This is disproportionation, $\text{Cl}$ is both oxidised to $+1$ in chloric(I) acid, $\text{HOCl}$, and reduced to $-1$ in hydrochloric acid, $\text{HCl}$.

Pick out the active disinfectant**
$\text{HOCl}$ (which partly ionises to $\text{ClO}^{-}$) is the active species. It kills bacteria and other pathogens, so the water is safe to drink.

Final answer: $\text{Cl}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{HCl} + \text{HOCl}$
$\text{HOCl}$ / $\text{ClO}^{-}$ kills bacteria / disinfects water.

hints: Remember that reducing power of halide ions increases down the group, so which halide can reduce sulfur from +6 all the way to -2 in $\text{H}_2\text{S}$?
walkthrough:
Use the reducing series**
$\text{I}^{-}$ is the strongest reducing agent of $\text{Cl}^{-}$, $\text{Br}^{-}$, $\text{I}^{-}$. Only iodide is strong enough to reduce concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ right down to $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ (sulfur oxidation state $+6$ to $-2$). So the salt is $\text{NaI}$.
Final answer: sodium iodide / $\text{NaI}$

hints: Think about which halide ion is too weak a reducing agent to reduce sulfur at all, so only proton transfer to make HX occurs.
walkthrough:
Spot the non-reducing halide**
$\text{Cl}^{-}$ cannot reduce $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$. It only accepts a proton:
$$\text{NaCl} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{NaHSO}_4 + \text{HCl}$$
That is Bronsted-Lowry acid-base only, with steamy white fumes of $\text{HCl}$. So the answer is $\text{NaCl}$.
Final answer: sodium chloride / $\text{NaCl}$

hints: Recall the three silver halide precipitate colours for chloride (white), bromide and iodide, and place bromide in the middle.
walkthrough:
Apply the silver nitrate test**
$$\text{Ag}^{+}(\text{aq}) + \text{Br}^{-}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{AgBr}(\text{s})$$
Silver bromide is the middle colour: white ($\text{AgCl}$), cream ($\text{AgBr}$), yellow ($\text{AgI}$). So you see a cream or off-white precipitate.
Final answer: cream(-coloured) / off-white precipitate / solid forms

hints: Check the electronegativity values in Table 3.1 for Br (2.8) and I (2.5) to decide if $\text{IBr}$ is non-polar like $\text{Br}_2$ or polar, then remember which force is present in all molecules.
walkthrough:
Combine the universal force with the polar force**
All molecules have London (instantaneous dipole-induced dipole) forces from shifting electron clouds. $\text{IBr}$ is also polar because I ($2.5$) and Br ($2.8$) have different electronegativities, so there is a permanent dipole. Polar molecules also attract by permanent dipole-permanent dipole forces. Both types act between $\text{IBr}$ molecules.
Final answer: instantaneous dipole-induced dipole / London / dispersion forces AND permanent dipole-permanent dipole forces

hints: Remember the standard two-word name for the mechanism where the pi bond of an alkene like propene attacks an electrophile such as $\text{HBr}$ or $\text{IBr}$.
walkthrough:
Name the alkene pathway**
Propene has an electron-rich $\text{C=C}$ double bond that donates to an electrophile, then a nucleophile adds in the second step. That two-step pathway is electrophilic addition, the same as $\text{HBr}$ + propene.

hints: Write propene as $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CH}_2$ and remember both atoms of $\text{IBr}$ add across the double bond to give a saturated three-carbon chain.
Swap the positions of I and Br on carbons 1 and 2 to generate the two possible addition products, keeping one halogen on each of the original double-bond carbons.
walkthrough:
Add I and Br across the double bond**
Start with $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CH}_2$. Addition breaks the pi bond and puts one atom of $\text{IBr}$ on each of the two alkene carbons. Carbon 3 ($\text{CH}_3$) is unchanged.

Draw both arrangements**
Isomer 1: I on the middle carbon, Br on the end carbon: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(I)CH}_2\text{Br}$ (1-bromo-2-iodopropane).
Isomer 2: Br on the middle carbon, I on the end carbon: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(Br)CH}_2\text{I}$ (2-bromo-1-iodopropane).
Final answer: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(I)CH}_2\text{Br}$ AND $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(Br)CH}_2\text{I}$

hints: Think about what is the same (carbon skeleton and functional groups) and what differs (where I and Br sit on the chain) to choose between chain, positional and functional group isomerism.
walkthrough:
Classify the difference**
Both molecules have the same skeleton, propane, with one Br and one I. Only the positions of the halogens differ. That is positional isomerism, also called regioisomerism.
Final answer: position(al) / regio- (isomerism)

hints: Recall that in electrophilic addition to propene two different carbocations can form, a primary and a secondary, and one is more stable.
Use the electronegativity difference between I (2.5) and Br (2.8) to work out which end of $\text{I}^{\delta+}-\text{Br}^{\delta-}$ acts as the electrophile and adds first.
walkthrough:
Find the electrophile in polar IBr**
Br is more electronegative than I, so $\text{IBr}$ is $\text{I}^{\delta+}-\text{Br}^{\delta-}$. The electron-rich $\text{C=C}$ attacks $\text{I}^{\delta+}$, so I bonds first and $\text{Br}^{-}$ adds second.

Compare the two possible carbocations**
If I adds to the end carbon ($\text{CH}_2$), the positive charge lands on the middle carbon, giving a secondary carbocation $[\text{CH}_3\text{CHCH}_2\text{I}]^{+}$. If I adds to the middle carbon, a primary carbocation forms. Secondary carbocations are stabilised by more electron-donating alkyl groups, so the secondary intermediate forms faster and its product dominates. Hence unequal amounts, a Markovnikov-type preference.

Final answer: $\text{IBr}$ is polar with $\text{I}^{\delta+}$ / I attacks first as the electrophile.
The secondary carbocation / $[\text{CH}_3\text{CHCH}_2\text{I}]^{+}$ intermediate is more stable and is preferred, so one product pathway is favoured.
